![The 2-versus-7 ambiguity that motivates the paper: given a training set of clean 2s and 7s, the smudged middle image should receive much lower confidence than the two flanking it. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In *Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness* [[1]](#ref-1) (ICML 1999), [Volodya Vovk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Vovk), [Alex Gammerman](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=uoWoR4gAAAAJ), and [Craig Saunders](https://dblp.org/pid/66/4053.html) at Royal Holloway, University of London unify their earlier transduction work into a single scheme based on the notion of algorithmic randomness — one of the founding papers of what is now called [conformal prediction](/posts/20260505-conformal-prediction-primer/). The complaint that opens the paper is that most learning algorithms output a bare prediction with no measure of how much to trust it, and that the example a classifier is least sure about is exactly the one a user most needs flagged.

The paper rests on two quantities, and the rest of it is about how to compute them. Each candidate label $Y$ gets a *p-value* $p(Y) \in [0, 1]$ measuring how well that labeling fits the training data. The $p(Y)$ across labels are separate tail probabilities, one per candidate-label hypothesis, not a distribution over labels, and they need not sum to 1. The prediction is the label with the largest p-value, $\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)$:

- **Confidence** $= 1 - p_{(2)}$, where $p_{(2)}$ is the second-largest p-value across the candidate labels. High confidence means every label other than the predicted one fits the data poorly, so the prediction is unlikely to be wrong at the corresponding error level.
- **Credibility** $= \max_Y p(Y) = p(\hat{y})$, how well the *best* available label fits the data at all. Low credibility flags an input unlike anything in the training set: either the data are not [exchangeable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchangeable_random_variables) or the test example is unrepresentative, regardless of how confident the prediction looks.

The pair separates two failure modes that a single probability hides. A prediction can be confident but have low credibility — a signal that the input itself is strange, not just that the label is uncertain.

## The abstract

> Most machine learning algorithms share the following drawback: they only output bare predictions but not the confidence in those predictions. In the 1960s algorithmic information theory supplied *universal measures of confidence* but these are, unfortunately, *non-computable*. In this paper we combine the ideas of *algorithmic information theory* with the theory of *Support Vector machines* to obtain *practicable approximations to universal measures of confidence*. We show that in some standard problems of pattern recognition our approximations work well.

## Methods

The construction has three layers, and only the third one runs on a computer.

**The ideal, non-computable target.** A *p-value function*, or *randomness level*, scores how well a data sequence fits the independent-and-identically-distributed (iid) assumption: large when the sequence looks like a typical iid draw, small when it contains a pattern an iid source would rarely produce. ("Random" here is the algorithmic sense of "indistinguishable from a fair-coin sample," not the colloquial "erratic.") To classify a test point $x_{l+1}$, the ideal algorithm tries every candidate label, completes the sequence $(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_{l+1}, Y)$, and measures the randomness level $p(Y)$ of each completion. It predicts the label whose completion has the largest randomness level, $\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)$ — the label that makes the data look most consistent with iid, hence the least anomalous. *Credibility* is that largest randomness level, $p(\hat{y})$, and *confidence* is one minus the second-largest, $1 - p_{(2)}$.

The second-largest is what matters because the valid prediction set at significance level $\varepsilon$ is $\Gamma^{\varepsilon} = \{\,Y : p(Y) > \varepsilon\,\}$, and this is the single label $\hat{y}$ only when *every* alternative is rejected. That is an AND across the other labels, so the binding constraint is the largest of their p-values: $\max_{Y \neq \hat{y}} p(Y) = p_{(2)} \le \varepsilon$. So $1 - p_{(2)}$ is the highest confidence at which the predictor commits to one label. The error guarantee falls out of validity: each $p(Y)$ is a genuine p-value, so $\Pr[\,p(Y) \le \varepsilon\,] \le \varepsilon$ under the hypothesis that $Y$ is correct, and because a wrong prediction means the true label is the rejected one, it has probability at most $1 - \text{confidence}$. Credibility plays the complementary role: a small $p(\hat{y})$ means even the best label is atypical, flagging the input rather than the label.

The trouble is that the universal measures of randomness from [Kolmogorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrey_Kolmogorov) [[2]](#ref-2) and [Martin-Löf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_Martin-L%C3%B6f) [[3]](#ref-3) are non-computable — they can be approximated from below but never evaluated exactly.

**The Support Vector approximation.** To get something computable, the paper borrows Vapnik's Support Vector Machine (SVM) [[4]](#ref-4). Solving the SVM's dual optimization assigns each example a Lagrange multiplier $\alpha_i$ that grows with how hard the example is to fit. The earlier "Learning by Transduction" paper (Gammerman, Vapnik, and Vovk [[5]](#ref-5)) turned multipliers into a score with $f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign} \alpha$. The [companion paper](/posts/20260603-transduction-confidence-credibility/) (Saunders, Gammerman, and Vovk [[6]](#ref-6)) turns them into a p-value by ranking: sort the multipliers in decreasing order, and the p-value of a completion is the rank of the test example's multiplier divided by $l+1$. A genuinely strange or mislabelled example earns a large multiplier, ends up near the top of the ranking, and so gets a small p-value.

**The experiment.** The test bed is United States Postal Service (USPS) handwritten digits (LeCun et al. [[7]](#ref-7)), each a $16 \times 16$ image, with a two-class problem separating the digit 2 from the digit 7. The classifier is an SVM with a degree-3 polynomial kernel $K(x, x') = (x \cdot x')^3 / 256$, trained on 400 examples and evaluated on 100 single-example test sets.

## Results

- **Confidence and credibility separate correct from incorrect predictions** (Figure 2, credibility on the vertical axis, confidence on the horizontal). With $f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign}\alpha$, the 100 predictions split into two clusters by average credibility: a cluster of 93 correct examples is at credibility 1.0 and average confidence 0.902, while the cluster holding the single error (plus 6 correct examples) is at credibility 0.091. Credibility, not confidence, is what marks the examples the classifier should not be trusted on.
- **The choice of score function $f(\alpha)$ matters.** The $f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign}\alpha$ rule from the transduction paper suffers a "distortion phenomenon" and predicts worse. Switching to $f(\alpha) = \alpha$ or $f(\alpha) = \alpha^2$ pushes average confidence above 0.99 on the correct cluster while keeping the error cluster's credibility low.
- **The error bound is $\log(l + 1)$.** For a single test example, the randomness deficiency of a wrongly-labelled sequence is at most $\log(l+1)$, and the paper notes this matches the $l+1$ denominator in Vapnik's statistical learning theory and in PAC-style error bounds — the same quantity obtained from the algorithmic-randomness side.

![Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.jpg){fig-align="center"}

The paper closes with a set of impossibility results (Section 6). Under the iid assumption alone:

- **On-line prediction at every step is impossible** (§6.1). If both the data sequence and the stopping time are random, inequality (9) shows that even the *wrong* labeled sequence has a random continuation under iid — so under iid alone there is no way to rule out wrong predictions at a randomly chosen time. The paper offers this as the technical explanation for why machine learning under iid has stayed in the batch setting. **Practical impact:** conformal prediction's coverage guarantee holds at fixed batches, not at adversarially chosen stopping times. Streaming pipelines that need valid coverage at every step need assumptions stronger than iid.
- **Density estimation in high dimensions is impossible** (§6.2). When the input dimension is large compared to the sample size, the unlabelled $x_i$ are typically all distinct. Under iid, for any generating distribution $P$ there is a degenerate $P^*$ that places $y \mid x$ entirely on $-1$ or $+1$ for each $x$ but is indistinguishable from $P$ on the sample. So $P(y_{l+1} = 1 \mid x_{l+1})$ cannot be estimated to anything narrower than $\{0, 1\}$ without strictly stronger assumptions. **Practical impact:** conformal prediction returns a prediction *set* (the true label is among these) rather than a calibrated per-class probability like $P(\text{class A} \mid x) = 0.73$. The latter is provably out of reach in high dimensions under iid alone.
- **Regression as conditional-expectation estimation reduces to density estimation** (§6.3). Estimating $\mathbb{E}[y_{l+1} \mid x_{l+1}]$ under iid coincides with density estimation in the binary case, so the §6.2 impossibility transfers. Under a different framing, where $x_i$ are deterministic and only $y_i$ are stochastic, even pattern recognition becomes impossible without additional assumptions. **Practical impact:** conformal regression methods deliver prediction *intervals* (a calibrated band around $y$) rather than calibrated point estimates of $\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]$, for the same reason.

## What came after

The scheme here is transductive — to score a test example it effectively retrains for every candidate label, which is expensive — and the nonconformity signal is tied to the SVM. The work that followed relaxed both.

- **The general form.** Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer's *Algorithmic Learning in a Random World* [[8]](#ref-8) consolidated the theory into a form where any nonconformity score, not just an SVM multiplier, drives the calibration.
- **Split conformal prediction.** Papadopoulos et al. [[9]](#ref-9) replaced the per-label retraining with a single held-out calibration set, cheap enough to wrap around any pre-trained model — the form most practitioners use today.
- **Workarounds for the impossibility results.** Each of the §6 impossibilities has a follow-up that recovers what is possible without violating the underlying constraint:
  - **On-line prediction (§6.1):** Adaptive Conformal Inference (Gibbs and Candès [[13]](#ref-13)) updates the conformal threshold over time, holding long-run coverage under distribution shift. The new guarantee is a long-run coverage rate rather than per-step validity, which is why the §6.1 impossibility does not apply.
  - **Density estimation in high dimensions (§6.2):** Venn–Abers predictors (Vovk and Petej [[11]](#ref-11)) output a calibrated probability *interval* rather than a single number. An interval is what is achievable under iid alone in high dimensions, where the §6.2 impossibility blocks single-number probabilities.
  - **Regression (§6.3):** Conformalized quantile regression (Romano, Patterson, and Candès [[10]](#ref-10)) reformulates the task as quantile estimation and returns calibrated, locally adaptive prediction *intervals*. The impossibility blocks point estimates of $\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]$, not interval coverage, so quantile regression sidesteps it.
- **The deep-learning revival.** Angelopoulos and Bates' tutorial [[12]](#ref-12) repackaged the framework for deep learning and drove the recent wave of distribution-free uncertainty work — including the [conformal factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) and [conformal language modeling](/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/) methods built for language models.

## My Notes

- **The middle layer is the IJCAI companion paper.** This paper has three layers (ideal non-computable target, computable SVM approximation, experiment), and the middle layer comes from the same trio's IJCAI 1999 paper [[6]](#ref-6) on transduction with confidence and credibility. That paper introduces the SVM-rank-of-multipliers construction standalone, while this one wraps the same construction in algorithmic-randomness theory and adds the impossibility results.
- **Mapping to LLM prediction.** The paper picks the predicted label via $\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)$ and exposes the value at that argmax as *credibility*, $\max_Y p(Y) = p(\hat{y})$. LLM token prediction does the same operation, $\hat{y} = \arg\max_y p_{\text{softmax}}(y \mid x)$, with the max softmax as the value at the argmax. So when an LLM is described as "95% confident in its prediction," that 95% is colloquially called confidence but is structurally the paper's credibility. The paper's *confidence* ($1 - p_{(2)}$, one minus the second-largest p-value) is a different number with no common LLM analog. Wrapping conformal prediction around the LLM uses $1 - p_{\text{softmax}}(y \mid x)$ as the nonconformity score on a held-out [calibration set](/posts/20260505-conformal-prediction-primer/), and the result has the coverage guarantee the raw max softmax lacks.
